prompt: Why is the Banker's algorithm rarely used in general-purpose operating systems? Select all that apply.

options.text: Programs rarely know their maximum resource needs in advance
options.explanation: Correct. A web server thread can't say how many locks, buffers or file handles it will need. Without `Max`, the algorithm can't run.

options.text: Dynamic process creation requires registering maximum claims and preserving the safety invariant
options.explanation: Correct. Arrivals and departures add resource-manager bookkeeping; a new process can be admitted if its claims preserve safety.

options.text: A safety check costs O(m·n²), which adds up on every request with thousands of threads
options.explanation: Correct. Here n is the number of processes and m the number of resource types. With 5,000 threads, the squared thread count is 25 million, so that is tens of millions of comparisons per resource type per request in the worst case.

options.text: It can't guarantee freedom from deadlock
options.explanation: It does guarantee it, provided the declared maximums are honest and every process eventually finishes. Its problems are practicality and cost, not correctness.

options.text: It refuses some requests that would never have led to deadlock
options.explanation: Correct. Unsafe isn't deadlocked. Being conservative wastes capacity, since processes often never reach their maximums.

workedExample: Known credible maxima, consistently locked state accounting and repeated safety checks can be expensive or impractical. New processes require safe admission rather than a permanently fixed population. The algorithm preserves its resource-safety invariant under its assumptions, but it may defer requests that would have completed safely in hindsight. Kubernetes requests illustrate capacity reservation, not maximum-claim Banker semantics.
